stories.headline: Delhi High Court directs responses in AITA governance and election dispute by November 6
stories.title: Delhi High Court directs responses in AITA governance and election dispute by November 6
stories.summary: In the hearing held on September 25, the order of which was released recently, the High Court said that rejoinders, if any, to AITA’s replies should be filed by November 6.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Delhi High Court has asked the All India Tennis Association (AITA) and the original petitioners led by former player Somdev Devvarman to file replies to the Court-appointed administrator Justice (retd.) Gita Mittal’s request to implead the AITA Trust and the Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA) in the ongoing proceedings to amend the AITA’s Constitution.

In the hearing held on September 25, the order of which was released recently, the Court said that rejoinders, if any, to AITA’s replies should be filed by November 6, the date when the matter will be heard again.
Justice Mittal, in her report dated September 14, had alleged large-scale financial misconduct and accused the office-bearers of stonewalling requests for documents and information.

The Court has also asked the AITA to respond to the request to produce the complete minutes of the Extraordinary General Meeting held on July 26 to ratify the new Constitution in line with the National Sports Governance Act, 2025.
The timeline for the conduct of fresh elections has been extended to November 27 from the previous deadline of September 30.

The AITA had requested the extension to complete the various mandatory administrative processes in the lead-up to the elections, chief among which is the finalisation of the 40-member strong Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) roster.

stories.headline: Legal Immunity For CEC, ECs: Supreme Court notice to Centre, ECI
stories.title: Legal Immunity For CEC, ECs: Supreme Court notice to Centre, ECI
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has issued notice to the Centre and Election Commission on an ADR petition challenging Section 16 of the 2023 law that grants immunity to the CEC and ECs from civil and criminal proceedings.
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: 2 independent source groups -> high confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The plea seeks revival of proceedings against current and past CEC/Election Commissioners.

The Supreme Court today issued notice on a petition filed by the Association for Democratic Reforms challenging the immunity granted to Chief Election Commissioner/Election Commissioners for actions taken in purported discharge of official duties.

A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana sought the response of the Union and the Election Commission on ADR's challenge to the constitutional validity of Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan appeared for ADR.
The petition has been filed through AoR Rani Mishra.
Briefly put, the petition seeks a declaration that Section 16 of the CEC Act is unconstitutional, void and inoperative as violative of Articles 14 and 21 and the basic structure of the Constitution.
It further seeks revival of proceedings against the present and past CEC and Election Commissioners, which came to an end as Section 16 of the CEC Act came into effect.

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no Court shall entertain or continue any civil or criminal proceedings against any person who is or was a Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner for any act, thing or word, committed, done or spoken by him when, or in the course of acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty or function."
The petition contends that Section 16 provides blanket immunity to the current and previous CEC/ECs for lifetime, which has no rational nexus with the objective of ensuring independence of CEC/ECs.
The provision places the CEC & ECs beyond the reach of any Court of law, it highlights.
"No other provision in the Constitution of India or any statute grants immunity that is at once lifelong, unconditioned by good faith, free of any sanction mechanism, and without a saving clause."
Petitioner-ADR further points out that Section 16 was not originally part of the Bill introduced.

stories.title: From Boat Club lawns to Jantar Mantar: How Delhi's protest map has changed

However, given the booking cost and availability of Ramlila Maidan, as of Tuesday, protestors have returned to Jantar Mantar.Before Jantar Mantar became the city’s best-known venue for demonstrations, the Boat Club lawns near India Gate drew mass gatherings. while India Gate and Raisina Hill became focal points for public anger at other times. Jantar Mantar.

After demonstrations at the Boat Club were restricted, Jantar Mantar became a regular location for citizens, political groups, unions and activists to hold demonstrations.
It is close to Parliament but smaller and easier to regulate than the Boat Club lawns.
Recent significant protests held here include the 2011 hunger fast by Anna Hazare, the One Rank.
One Pension agitation in 2015, where former servicemen demanded full implementation of the One Rank.
One Pension scheme, and the 2017, Tamil Nadu farmers’ protest seeking loan waivers, drought relief, and a Cauvery Management Board to oversee the sharing of river water between states.

Post-Covid agitations at this venue include the January 2023 protest by national wrestlers including Vinesh Phogat, Sakshi Malik and Bajrang Punia who alleged sexual harassment and misconduct by then Wrestling Federation of India president Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh, and the ongoing protest over electoral rolls by the CJP and other groups.
India Gate and Raisina Hill: Protests over women’s safety.

The gang rape of a 23-year-old woman in a moving bus in Delhi on December 16, 2012, triggered days of protests across the capital.
Students and other citizens gathered at India Gate and around Raisina Hill to demand justice for the victim and stronger action against sexual violence.
India Gate and Raisina Hill were not designated protest venues.
Sant Nirankari Samagam Ground, Burari, North Delhi; Photo by Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesBurari: Proposed venue during farmers’ protests.
When: November 2020Where: Sant Nirankari Samagam Ground, Burari, north DelhiBurari became a protest venue for farmers demanding the repeal of three farm laws passed by Parliament in 2020.
As farmers from Punjab marched towards the capital, police offered this location to hold their demonstrations.
However, many refused to move to Burari and instead camped for more than a year at the Singhu and Tikri borders.

stories.headline: Delhi SIR : Plea In Supreme Court Challenges ECI Directive That Deleted Voters Must File Form 6 For Electoral Roll Registration
stories.title: Delhi SIR : Plea In Supreme Court Challenges ECI Directive That Deleted Voters Must File Form 6 For Electoral Roll Registration
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: A plea has been filed in the Supreme Court challenging the Election Commission of India's procedure in the Delhi Special Intensive Revision requiring voters, whose names have been deleted pursuant to the SIR exercise, to fill Form 6 to seek re-inclusion of their names on the voter list.

An interlocutory application petition has been filed by transparency Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri through Advocate Prashant Bhushan in the pending petition, where they have challenged procedures regarding a logical discrepancy in the Delhi SIR.
The petition has been filed through Advocate Prashant Bhushan and Neha Rathi.
They have pointed out that Form 6 requires every applicant to affirm that they are “applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the first time”.

It has stated that during the enumeration phase of the Special Intensive Revision(SIR) in Delhi, 47,56,722 electors (32.78% of the voters who existed prior to the start of SIR) were excluded from the Draft Electoral Roll under the category of ASDD (Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate).
For any person on the ASDD list, the only mechanism for filing a claim for having their name restored in the voter list is through Form 6.

The petitioners have pointed out that this creates a fundamental anomaly as all these people were previously enrolled on the voter list but are now required to submit Form 6 and make a declaration that they are seeking inclusion in the electoral roll for the first time, which is factually incorrect and wholly inapplicable to their circumstances.

Further, such persons would also become liable for facing punishment for giving a declaration under Section 31 of the RP Act, 1950 which provides for imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.

The petition also points out that the additional Declaration Form required to be submitted along with Forms 6 and 8, which has been prescribed through the SIR guidelines, is without the force of law and should be struck down.
Form 6 is prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, which have been framed under Section 28 of the RPA, 1950.

Section 28(1) empowers the Central Government, after consultation with the Election Commission, to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act by notification in the Official Gazette, while Section 28(3) requires such rules to be laid before both Houses of Parliament and permits Parliament to modify or annul the same.
However, no such procedure was followed for this additional declaration form.

stories.headline: Supreme Court asks Delhi governmente to seek inputs from IB on Hawara plea for transfer to Punjab jail
stories.title: Supreme Court asks Delhi governmente to seek inputs from IB on Hawara plea for transfer to Punjab jail
stories.summary: Bench takes a cautious approach, saying the case of Beant Singh murder convict is sensitive, and even the Punjab government seems to be reluctant
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) asked the Delhi government to seek inputs from the Intelligence Bureau (IB) on Beant Singh murder convict Jagtar Singh Hawara’s plea for transfer from Delhi’s Tihar jail to a prison in Punjab.
A Bench headed by Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale took a cautious approach, saying the case was sensitive, and even the Punjab government seemed to be reluctant.
“We know that every sinner has a future… Like how somebody said, if you kill a single person, you are a murderer.
Kill a few thousand, you are a conqueror… But we will have to look at the implications of the transfer on the society,” Justice Sundresh said.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Delhi government, informed the top court that Hawara was involved in a jailbreak and his death penalty was converted to life imprisonment in the murder case.
Contending that transfer might increase chances of his escape, Ms. Bhati referred to an advisory by the Ministry of Home Affairs on transfer of high-risk prisoners.
Senior advocate Colin Gonsalves, for Hawara, said he had personally visited his client in jail and found him completely reformed.
Ms. Bhati referred to a Punjab government affidavit which sounded apprehensive about the effect of Hawara’s shift on the law and order situation in the State.
Mr. Gonsalves submitted that the assassination of the Chief Minister happened in 1995 when his client was only 21 years old.
“His mother is very old, 82 years old and in serious condition.
He is only seeking a transfer to a Punjab high-security prison, and not seeking release.
He has a blemishless record in jail,” Mr. Gonsalves argued.

stories.headline: Chips will matter in the long term: N Chandrasekaran, Tata Sons chief
stories.title: Chips will matter in the long term: N Chandrasekaran, Tata Sons chief
stories.summary: Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran said that semiconductor chips are the future and will be required in the long run, irrespective of how soon India makes them, while speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi on Tuesday. Referring to Tata Sons' subsidiary Tata Electronics' attempt to manufacture chips for automotive, artificial intelligence (AI) applications and other uses, he added: "Whether we will get it right and hit the numbers in two years or three years is not the point. The point is chips are going to be fundamentally required." He said the company will continue to check on the demand and financial viability for the development, and it was difficult to have a clean spreadsheet in the current environment of uncertainty.Also Read: AI job anxiety comments are disaster marketing, says Nandan NilekaniWhile the world faces technology and fiscal disruptions, the way to progress would be to build resilient businesses that are derisked from dependence on a single geography, observed other industry experts who were part of a panel discussion with Chandrasekaran. “I continue to think technology probably is the biggest existential risk, but another risk is the lack of fiscal sustainability in Western governments,” said Jonathan Gray, president and chief operating officer at Blackstone. He added that emerging market countries were more responsible in many cases, and the moment of reckoning was playing out in the turbulent bond markets.While the current global environment offers governments around the world an opportunity to subsidise or incentivise resilience, one must be careful, said Rishi Sunak, former UK Prime Minister and member of parliament. “Politicians always like opportunities to protect local businesses. They like opportunities to put up barriers that protect the producers, and this gives them an excuse to do that,” he said.Also Read: Tata Sons chairman outlines three steps for sustained economic growthDrawing from his experience at G7, Sunak said the notion of derisking rather than decoupling, with “high fence for a small garden” floated by Jake Sullivan, then US National Security Advisor, captures the idea of prioritising national sovereign capability in critical sectors.Chandrasekaran said that while the world is still coming to terms with the tech disruption caused by AI, its impact in the long term is going to be powerful. He added that in a volatile environment, optimising for efficiency wasn’t the right approach, and neither was resilience opposed to efficiency. “To think that resilience is opposite of efficiency is a problem. I believe if you design it [systems] for resilience in an unpredictable environment, you're actually optimising for efficiency. You look at our business; we have seen supply chain disruptions across industries... Any disruption halts production,” he said. “It really surprises me how well we have done as a group with so many disruptions. We had an air crash. We had a cyber-attack. We had supply chain disruptions. Still, as a group, we will deliver the money, and margins are already done.”Gray said the firm wanted to continue to bet on electricity to power technology, data centres, autonomous vehicles, robots and other tech advancements. He added that AI will be moving from the desktop to the physical world, with self-reliant tech advancements taking precedence, such as defence and life science, where Blackstone plans on doubling down. “It will be good for India but the benefit to human health is going to be the number one thing coming out of it,” he said. “With new infrastructure in place, India will grow faster than any other major economy in the world and we are looking to deploy more capital in the geography for the next part of the century.”

He added that in a volatile environment, optimising for efficiency wasn’t the right approach, and neither was resilience opposed to efficiency.
“To think that resilience is opposite of efficiency is a problem.
I believe if you design it [systems] for resilience in an unpredictable environment, you're actually optimising for efficiency.
You look at our business; we have seen supply chain disruptions across industries...
Any disruption halts production,” he said.
“It really surprises me how well we have done as a group with so many disruptions.
We had an air crash.
We had a cyber-attack.
We had supply chain disruptions.

Still, as a group, we will deliver the money, and margins are already done.” Gray said the firm wanted to continue to bet on electricity to power technology, data centres, autonomous vehicles, robots and other tech advancements.

He added that AI will be moving from the desktop to the physical world, with self-reliant tech advancements taking precedence, such as defence and life science, where Blackstone plans on doubling down.
“It will be good for India but the benefit to human health is going to be the number one thing coming out of it,” he said.
“With new infrastructure in place, India will grow faster than any other major economy in the world and we are looking to deploy more capital in the geography for the next part of the century.”

sentences.text: Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran said that semiconductor chips are the future and will be required in the long run, irrespective of how soon India makes them, while speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi on Tuesday.

“I continue to think technology probably is the biggest existential risk, but another risk is the lack of fiscal sustainability in Western governments,” said Jonathan Gray, president and chief operating officer at Blackstone.
